newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran president Khatami's political honeymoon over.
newsitem.headline: Iran president Khatami's political honeymoon over.

text.p: Iranian President Mohammad Khatami has had the briefest of political honeymoons as his differences with political opponents are coming out in the open.
Analysts and diplomats said on Thursday said the moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric was facing a stern challenge by conservative opponents over his choice of some key cabinet ministers.
The 54-year-old president had also inherited an economy that was showing early signs of a possible slowdown and an electorate filled with high expectations of change, they added.

Conservatives and hardliners, who had largely refrained from publicly criticising Khatami since his election in May, have opened up with harsh attacks on his cabinet choices ahead of a parliamentary debate on Tuesday.
"It is now certain that a noteworthy number of these nominees will not be able to get the parliament's vote of confidence," the Tehran Times newspaper said on Thursday.
Some analysts said that the 270-seat parliament, or Majlis, was expected to approve the majority of Khatami's 22-member cabinet but vote against proposed culture minister Ataollah Mohajerani.
Mohajerani has been criticised by conservative for his advocacy of greater cultural freedoms and his call in 1990 for direct talks with the United States.
"Introducing a person like Mohajerani who seeks relations with America is an insult to the Majlis," deputy Mehdi-Reza Darvishzadeh told Resalat newspaper on Thursday.
But the daily Ettelaat said a group of writers and artists had written to Khatami backing Mohajerani's nomination.
The culture ministry plays a key role in domestic life in Iran since it has oversight over what books and films can be printed and the extent of media freedom.
Conservatives are also expected to question the nomination as interior minister of Abdollah Nouri, a cleric deputy who leads a pro-Khatami faction in parliament, analysts said.

Khatami's choice of United Nations ambassador Kamal Kharrazi as foreign minister has also been attacked by hardliners who question his revolutionay credentials for having lived a long time in the United States, a country whose government is the Islamic republic's arch-foe.

Khatami was swept into power in national elections in May after scooping the votes of Iranian youth, women and middle classes who saw in him a leader able to inject social and economic freedoms to the stern Islamic state.

From his election victory to his swearing in ceremony on August 4, Khatami raised the possibility of changes in normal peoples' daily lives and that his administration could herald a change in Iran's foreign relations.
Khatami fought back attacks on his nominees with a televised nationwide address on Wednesday night saying that he was determined to press through his programme backed by a strong electoral mandate.
"I have a pact with the people to fulfil my plans," he said in his first major interview since taking office.
Khatami also used the address to call for the creation of an independent press and formal political parties, not allowed by authorities since the years after the 1979 revolution.
Parliament is led by speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri whom Khatami crushed at the elections, getting nearly 20 million votes compared to Nateq-Nouri's seven million.
"The conservatives are still smarting from their election defeat...They want their day too," said one diplomat.
Khatami said he would respect parliament decisions and that he had a list of alternatives for cabinet posts.
He also suggested that a woman would be in his cabinet as a vice president, a position which does not need parliamentary approval.
Iran's economic health will also be of concern to Khatami as evidence comes through that government revenues have fallen below budget forecast and that prices continue to rise.
The president said that work would quickly begin on a new budget which would be presented to the parliament in November.

Iranian Deputy Oil Minister Hojatollah Ghanimifard told Reuters on Thursday that petroleuml revenue -- the lifeblood of the economy -- was running behind budget expectations because of weaker international oil prices since March.
